Why Do New Business Ideas Come About?

Business is dynamic — it never stands still. The products and services people want today are different from what they wanted five or ten years ago. The Edexcel specification identifies three main reasons why new business ideas emerge: changes in technology, changes in what consumers want, and products or services becoming obsolete.

Key Fact

Three reasons why new business ideas come about: changes in technology, changes in what consumers want, and products and services becoming obsolete.

Changes in Technology

New technology creates opportunities for entrepreneurs by making entirely new products and services possible. Smartphone app stores created the mobile-gaming market. Streaming platforms like Spotify disrupted CD and MP3 sales. GPS-enabled smartphones allowed businesses like Deliveroo to scale quickly, and contactless payments changed how customers pay in shops — roughly one in three UK adults now use their phone to pay at least once a month.

Technology also reduces costs. Automation cuts unit costs through speed and accuracy, meaning start-ups can charge lower prices or keep higher profit margins to help them grow. Amazon’s warehouses use robots, scanners, and software to control the schedule of packages — a level of efficiency that would be impossible without advanced technology.

E-commerce — buying and selling online via the internet. M-commerce — sales via smartphones and tablets. Automation — using technology to complete tasks with little human input. Obsolescence — when a product or service becomes out of date.

However, relying on new technology carries risk. If technology fails, production can halt, leading to lost sales and damage to the business’s reputation. A business must weigh the potential benefits of adopting new technology against the costs and risks involved.

Changes in What Consumers Want

Consumer tastes change over time, and businesses must keep up or risk losing sales. A consumer is the end user of a product or service. Their preferences shift because of factors like health trends, environmental concerns, social media influence, and changes in income.

Several recent trends show how consumer tastes are reshaping markets. Plant-based meals from brands like Quorn and Beyond Meat are replacing traditional meat products, driven by health, animal welfare, and climate concerns. The UK plant-based sector is experiencing double-digit annual growth. Sustainable packaging is another shift — 87% of shoppers say they will pay more for greener packaging, moving away from single-use plastic. Apps like Vinted and Depop have transformed second-hand fashion: over half of 18 to 24-year-olds have sold clothes online, and Vinted now has more users than ASOS Marketplace.

Key Fact

Streaming services show the scale of change: in 2015 just 1 in 5 UK homes had a service like Netflix, but by 2024 around 2 out of 3 homes (68%) subscribed to at least one streaming platform.

If a business ignores shifts in consumer taste, sales can fall as customers move to fresher alternatives. The business loses revenue and market share. Walkers, for example, responded to changing tastes by launching limited-edition sandwich-flavoured crisps, combining two lunchtime favourites to attract new customers.

Products and Services Becoming Obsolete

Obsolete means a product or service is no longer used because it has been replaced by something better. VHS cassettes are obsolete because consumers now stream films. Paper maps have been replaced by GPS systems and smartphone apps. Landline phones have largely disappeared as mobile phones offer greater convenience.

Typewriters replaced by computers. Film cameras replaced by digital cameras and smartphones. Floppy disks replaced by cloud storage and USB drives. Cassette tapes replaced by MP3 downloads and streaming. DVD rental shops (like Blockbuster) replaced by Netflix and other streaming services. Some services have also become obsolete — having film developed, renting videos from a shop, and chimney sweeping are all far less common today.

When a product becomes obsolete, demand falls and revenue drops. Customers switch to rivals with newer products, meaning the firm sells fewer units and finds it harder to cover its fixed costs. To survive, a business must either adapt its existing products or develop entirely new ones.

How New Business Ideas Come About

The specification identifies two ways new ideas emerge: original ideas and adapting existing products, services, or ideas.

An original idea is one that has not been used before. Art Fry invented the Post-it Note by accident when he needed something to keep the page open in his hymn book. Rob Law was just 21 when he combined a toy with luggage to create the Trunki suitcase — his company Magmatic now employs 80 people and has sold 2.8 million products in 100 countries. Tails.com spotted that 4 out of 5 UK dog owners treat their pet as part of the family, creating tailored dog food delivered to the door — they now have over 40,000 UK customers.

Key Fact

Original ideas often come from spotting a gap in the market (an unmet customer need) or solving a problem that no existing product addresses.

Adapting existing ideas means modifying a product to appeal to different customers or markets. This is less risky than launching something completely new because the original product was already successful. Examples include combining two products (a spork combines a spoon and a fork), creating newer versions of classic cars like the Ford Mustang, or McDonald’s changing its menu for different countries — offering a McBaguette with Dijon mustard in France. Aldi produces cheaper versions of designer clothing, making fashion accessible to more consumers.

The existing product was already successful for a period of time, so the business knows there is demand. Changes can often be made without major costs. The business invests less capital, so if the adapted product succeeds, more profit is made per product sold. It also allows the business to offer more choices to customers without starting from scratch.

What Is Risk in Business?

Every time someone starts a business, they are taking a risk. There is no guarantee that the business will succeed. The Edexcel specification groups the main risks into three categories: business failure, financial loss, and lack of security. Understanding these risks — and balancing them against potential rewards — is central to the decision every entrepreneur must make.

Key Fact

The three main risks of starting a business are: business failure (the business ceases to trade), financial loss (costs exceed revenue, and money invested is lost), and lack of security (no guaranteed income or employee benefits).

Business Failure

Business failure is when a business can no longer operate and closes permanently. Start-up failure rates are stark: 20% of small businesses fail in their first year, 30% fail by their second year, 50% fail within five years, and 70% fail by their tenth year.

Recent high-profile UK failures show that even well-known brands are not safe. Wilko (2023) ran out of cash and closed all 400+ stores. The Body Shop UK collapsed in February 2024. Ted Baker went bust in March 2024 after debts piled up. Claire’s UK went into administration in August 2025, putting 2,150 jobs at risk.

There are several common reasons why businesses fail:

Cash flow problems — the business cannot pay rent, wages, or suppliers on time. Wilko had the wrong stock and no cash coming in.

High costs and low sales — energy, rent, and wages rise while consumers cut back during the cost-of-living crisis. The Body Shop closed many stores for this reason.

Too much competition — cheaper high-street rivals like Primark and B&M, plus online giants such as Amazon and Shein, take customers away.

Changing consumer tastes — if a business does not keep up with trends, customers drift away. Ted Baker became less fashionable compared to newer brands.

Failure to innovate — products can become obsolete if the business does not adapt. Blockbuster failed because it did not move to streaming quickly enough.

Financial Loss

Financial loss occurs when a business’s costs exceed its revenue. An entrepreneur typically invests their own savings or borrows money from a bank to start up. If the business is not profitable, that money may never be recovered.

If the business is a sole trader or partnership, the owner has unlimited liability, meaning personal assets like a car or even a home could be used to pay business debts. This makes financial loss one of the most serious risks an entrepreneur faces.

Key Fact

Profit is the money left when total costs are subtracted from total revenue. If costs exceed revenue, the business makes a loss. For example, if an entrepreneur buys stock for £800 but only sells it for £600, they have made a £200 financial loss.

Lack of Security

Lack of security means the entrepreneur has no guaranteed wage, no paid holiday or sick pay, and no employer pension. If an entrepreneur leaves a regular job to start a business, they give up all of these protections.

Income depends entirely on sales, which can be unpredictable. In a slow month, the entrepreneur may be unable to pay personal bills such as a mortgage. Long hours and stress can also lead to burnout, and there is no safety net if the business struggles.

Beyond the three main risks, entrepreneurs also face:

Cyber attacks — small firms are collectively attacked seven million times per year in the UK, costing an estimated £5.26 billion. Malware, hacking, and ransomware can steal data, cause financial loss, and damage reputation.

Economic problems — in a recession, customers save rather than spend on non-essential items, reducing sales and profit.

Poor reputation — bad customer service or safety incidents can destroy trust. After the Smiler crash, Alton Towers was fined £5 million and visitor numbers took years to recover.

Supply chain failures — KFC had to close hundreds of UK branches in 2018 after switching supplier to DHL, which struggled with the delivery volume.

The Rewards of Enterprise

Despite the risks, there are strong reasons why people start businesses. The three main rewards are: profit, independence, and business success.

Profit — the entrepreneur keeps the profit the business generates. Unlike an employee on a fixed salary, there is no ceiling on what they can earn. However, they may need to reinvest some profit back into the business as equipment wears out, and if they take on a partner, profits must be shared.

Independence — being your own boss means making all the major decisions: what to sell, how to price it, when to work. The government lists better work autonomy, better work challenge, and family legacy (building a business to pass on) as key benefits. This control and freedom is a powerful motivator for many entrepreneurs.

Business success — a growing customer base, positive reviews, and a strong reputation bring personal satisfaction and status. The case study of Jamal Acharya shows this well: he started Web Horizons Ltd in 2018, grew it through positive reviews, signed contracts with large companies, and eventually reduced his hours to four days a week to spend more time with family.

Key Fact

The three main rewards are: profit (income for the owner if the business succeeds), independence (ability to make your own decisions and control your working life), and business success (personal satisfaction, reputation, and achievement).

Balancing Risk and Reward

Entrepreneurs can take steps to reduce risk before and during their business. Producing a business plan helps spot problems early. Cash-flow forecasting reveals when money might run short. Market research helps the entrepreneur understand what customers want and are willing to pay, lowering the chance of failure. Working closely with customers — as the Edexcel exam question suggests — is one of the most effective ways to reduce the risk of financial loss.

before.content_html:
The Purpose of Business Activity

Every business exists for three core reasons: to produce goods or services, to meet customer needs, and to add value. Understanding these purposes is essential for your Edexcel exam, because they explain why businesses are set up and how they survive in competitive markets.

Key Fact

The three purposes of business activity are: to produce goods or services, to meet customer needs, and to add value. These come directly from the Edexcel specification for 1.1.3.

Producing Goods and Services

To produce goods and services, a business needs four factors of production. These are land (a place to produce, such as a farm or factory), labour (people to work in the business), capital (money and equipment to get started), and enterprise (the drive and motivation from the owner to start and run the business).

A good is a physical product you can touch, such as a pair of trainers or a sausage roll. A service is something a business does for you, such as a haircut or a train journey. Most businesses produce one or both of these to earn revenue.

Meeting Customer Needs

Successful businesses focus on what their customers actually want. Common customer expectations include fast and efficient service, high-quality products at a competitive price, friendly and helpful staff, trained employees who can answer questions, and a clean shop or easy-to-navigate website.

If a business fails to meet these needs, customers will go to a competitor instead. For example, McDonald’s meets the need for speed and convenience through its drive-thru and mobile ordering app, while Waitrose meets the need for quality by selling premium and locally sourced food. Businesses that consistently meet customer expectations build a loyal customer base, which leads to repeat purchases and positive word-of-mouth recommendations.

What Is Added Value?

Added value is the difference between what a business pays its suppliers for materials and the price it charges customers for the finished product. For example, Starbucks pays around £0.60 for the coffee beans, milk, and cup for a medium latte, but sells it for £3.50 — giving an added value of £2.90. Similarly, a Greggs sausage roll costs just £0.25 in ingredients but sells for £1.20, creating £0.95 of added value through freshly baked convenience and high-street locations. Added value is important because it allows a business to cover its other costs and make a profit.

Key Fact

Added value = Selling price − Cost of inputs. Nike pays roughly £20 for materials to make Air Force 1 trainers but sells them for £110, creating £90 of added value through design, branding, and celebrity endorsements.

Five Ways to Add Value

The exam board identifies five methods businesses use to add value: convenience, branding, quality, design, and having a unique selling point (USP).

Branding — A strong brand creates customer loyalty and allows a business to charge more. Nike’s “Just Do It” slogan and swoosh logo mean customers pay a premium even when cheaper alternatives exist.

Design — An attractive or innovative product justifies a higher price. Apple MacBooks use sleek aluminium designs that make customers willing to pay more for the look and feel. Dyson’s bladeless fans use futuristic design to charge a premium for what is essentially a fan.

Quality — High-quality products reduce complaints and encourage repeat purchases. Barbour hand-crafts waxed jackets in the UK using durable materials — some are passed down through generations.

USP — A unique selling point differentiates a product from competitors. Innocent Smoothies’ USP is 100% natural ingredients with no added sugar, appealing to health-conscious consumers.

Convenience — Making things easier for the customer adds value. Amazon Prime offers next-day delivery, Tesco Click & Collect lets customers order online and pick up in store, and Uber allows instant ride booking via an app.

The Role of Entrepreneurship

An entrepreneur is someone who takes a business idea and turns it into reality. The exam board requires you to know three key roles of an entrepreneur: organising resources, making business decisions, and taking risks.

Organising resources — An entrepreneur brings together the four factors of production. Andrew Jennings, founder of Berrywhite organic drinks, had to organise raw materials, a factory, workers, and marketing before he could sell a single bottle.

Making business decisions — Entrepreneurs decide on the brand name, logo, core values, pricing, promotion methods, and where to get finance. These decisions shape whether the business succeeds or fails.

Taking risks — Setting up a business means paying out money in advance for materials, equipment, and wages with no guarantee the product will sell. If the business fails, the entrepreneur bears all the costs. Leaving a regular job to start a business means giving up a secure income.

Key Fact

Enterprise is about taking risks, being creative and innovative, and using initiative. It is one of the four factors of production and the driving force behind every new business.

before.content_html:
What Are Customer Needs?

In business, a customer need is a problem that customers could solve by purchasing a product or service. A good business will aim to satisfy these needs. The Edexcel specification identifies four key customer needs: price, quality, choice, and convenience.

Key Fact

The four customer needs you must know for your exam are: price (what the customer pays), quality (how good or reliable the product is), choice (the range of options available), and convenience (how easy and fast it is for the customer to buy).

Price

Price is how much a customer pays for a product or service. Customers want to feel they are getting good value for money — this does not always mean the cheapest option. Value for money means the quality of the product is fair relative to the price paid. For example, a student might choose the cheapest pair of trainers available, while a professional athlete might pay more for a pair that lasts longer and performs better.

Businesses must set prices carefully. If the price is too high, customers will buy from competitors. If the price is too low, the business may not cover its costs or customers may question the quality.

Quality

Quality means how good or reliable a product is and how well it meets customer expectations. By UK law, products must be of a “satisfactory quality” — this means the product must meet the standard that a reasonable person would regard as acceptable.

Quality is linked to price. A jacket costing £10 would not be expected to be the same quality as one costing £1,600. However, both must be satisfactory for their price point. Businesses like JD Sports stock trusted brands such as Nike and Adidas because customers associate these names with reliable, long-lasting products.

JD Sports (product-focused) targets 15–18-year-old students. It meets customer needs through: student discount periods and sale rails (price), trusted brands that last (quality), a wide range of sizes, colours, and styles (choice), and click-and-collect with easy returns (convenience).

A local barber (service-focused) targets working adults with limited time. It meets customer needs through: clear price lists and loyalty cards (price), trained barbers using quality products (quality), different services like skin fades and beard trims (choice), and walk-ins plus online booking with evening and Saturday hours (convenience).

Choice

Choice refers to the range of options customers can pick from. Not every customer wants the same product or service, so businesses often produce a product range to meet different needs. For example, a car manufacturer might offer an SUV for families, a small car for new drivers, and a sports car for customers who want luxury and performance.

Supermarkets are a good example of choice in action. A typical supermarket might stock over 400 types of yoghurt. While this seems excessive, it allows the business to cater to customers with different dietary requirements, taste preferences, and budgets. However, offering limited choice can also be a strategy — fewer options can help customers choose more quickly, reducing the chance they abandon their purchase.

Convenience

Customer convenience means saving the customer time and effort. The task of business owners is to find a way of trading that makes purchasing as easy as possible. Examples of convenience include: next-day delivery, personalisation of products, self-service checkouts, and choosing a good business location.

Key Fact

Deliveroo is a strong example of convenience. It offers home delivery from restaurants that do not provide their own delivery service, allowing customers to access high-quality restaurant food from the comfort of their own home or office.

Why Identifying Customer Needs Matters

Understanding customer needs is essential for two reasons the exam board requires you to know: generating sales and business survival.

Generating sales: A business needs to generate sales to survive. It can do this by lowering the price, promoting the product through advertising, running competitions or other promotional activities, and improving the product. Meeting customer needs directly leads to higher sales because satisfied customers are more likely to make purchases and return for repeat business.

Business survival: If a business does not identify and satisfy customer needs, it will not survive. The business must find out what customers want and need, then provide that product or service at the right price, in the right place, at the right time. If a rival serves customer needs better, market share can fall. Loyal customers help a business survive during downturns because they continue to buy even when times are difficult.

Key Fact

If a business fails to identify customer needs, it risks losing customers, gaining a bad reputation through negative reviews, falling sales revenue, and ultimately business failure through insolvency.

A business that understands its customers will offer a suitable product or service. This means the business will make sales and potentially boost profits. Businesses can check if they are meeting customer needs by monitoring sales figures, gathering customer feedback, and tracking repeat purchases.

Why Do Businesses Carry Out Market Research?

Market research is the process of finding out what customers want and need, and what competitors are doing. Without it, a business is guessing — and guessing costs money. The Edexcel spec identifies four key purposes of market research that you need to know.

Key Fact

The four purposes of market research are: to identify and understand customer needs, to identify gaps in the market, to reduce risk, and to inform business decisions.

A business uses market research to understand its potential and existing customers. For example, a clothing brand might discover through research that its target audience prefers sustainable fabrics. This is known as customer insight — smart clues about what people like, need, and why they buy.

Market research also helps businesses spot gaps in the market where no existing product meets customer needs. It reduces risk by testing ideas before a full launch. Greggs, for example, used social listening and in-store trials before rolling out its vegan sausage roll nationally — they tested small, measured actual buying behaviour, and only scaled up once demand was proven.

Primary Research Methods

Primary research (also called field research) involves collecting brand-new data directly from customers or potential customers. It is tailored to the business but tends to be more expensive and time-consuming than secondary research. Edexcel requires you to know four primary methods.

A survey is the whole process of planning, collecting, and analysing responses. A questionnaire is simply the set of questions used within a survey. Surveys can collect large amounts of data quickly — for example, satisfaction buttons in shops or pop-up forms on websites. Questionnaires are cost-efficient, especially online, and can be targeted at past customers. However, surveys may include poor-quality data (people pressing random buttons), and questionnaires often suffer from low return rates because customers dislike giving out personal details.

A focus group brings together a small group of potential customers to discuss a product or idea. It generates rich qualitative data about how customers feel. Disney, for example, uses kid-centric focus groups to test reactions to new characters and merchandise. The downside is that focus groups are expensive to organise, and dominant personalities can influence others’ responses.

Observation means watching how customers behave without them knowing — for example, tracking which route shoppers take around a store or whether they notice promotions. This gives accurate, natural data with no recall error, but it is very time-consuming and relies on the observer’s interpretation, which may be biased.

Secondary Research Methods

Secondary research (also called desk research) uses information that already exists. It is usually cheaper and faster than primary research, but may not be specific to the business. Edexcel requires you to know three secondary methods.

Key Fact

The three secondary research methods on the spec are: internet research (competitor websites, search trends, reviews), market reports (e.g. Mintel reports costing £1,000–£4,000), and government reports (e.g. the Office for National Statistics). All are cheaper than primary research but may be out of date or not specific to the business.

Internet research is free and available 24/7. A business can check competitor prices, read customer reviews, track search trends, and run A/B tests on its own website. Market reports from companies like Mintel compile detailed industry data — for example, showing that demand for high-protein snacks is rising, which might prompt a supermarket to launch a new product line. Government reports from the ONS provide demographic and industry data that helps businesses decide whether to expand into new areas.

Qualitative vs Quantitative Data

Quantitative data is numerical — statistics, percentages, and figures that can be displayed in charts. For example, “62% of respondents preferred delivery over click-and-collect.” It is useful for spotting patterns and making comparisons, but it does not explain why customers feel a certain way.

Qualitative data explores feelings and opinions — the “why” behind the numbers. Focus groups, interviews, and observation all generate qualitative data. Comments like “the burger was too salty but arrived fast” give a business specific, actionable feedback that numbers alone cannot provide.

Social media has transformed market research. It is cheaper than organising a focus group, provides real-time data, and reaches a much larger audience. Businesses can track trending hashtags, run Instagram polls, and monitor customer comments to spot emerging trends. However, not all social media data is reliable — responses may come from people outside the target market, and opinions can be influenced by viral trends rather than genuine preference.

Reliability of Market Research Data

Reliability means the research produces consistent results that could be repeated. If a business surveys only 40 people but has thousands of customers, the sample may be too small to be reliable. Validity means the research actually measures what it set out to measure — asking clear, unbiased questions to a representative sample.

Key Fact

Reliable research leads to informed decisions, reduced risk, and higher chances of success. Unreliable research can lead to launching products that do not sell, wasting money, and ultimately business failure.

What Is Market Segmentation?

Not every customer is the same. A teenager buying trainers has different needs to a retired couple looking for walking shoes. Market segmentation is the process of breaking down a whole market into smaller sub-groups so that a business can target the right customers with the right products.

Market research will show that a particular product appeals to a specific group of people. A business needs this information to identify groups with similar wants and needs. Once a business knows who its customers are, it can tailor its marketing, pricing, and product design to match.

Key Fact

The Edexcel spec requires you to know five ways of segmenting a market: location, demographics, lifestyle, income, and age. You also need to understand market mapping to identify gaps in the market and the competition.

Segmenting by Location

A business may decide to sell its product in just one country, one region, or in an even smaller area. Location segmentation means targeting customers based on where they live or where the product will be used. For example, a business selling raincoats would focus on rainy coastal areas like Cornwall or the Lake District, while a company selling beach towels would target seaside resort towns.

Businesses can also target urban versus rural areas. A food delivery app like Deliveroo focuses on cities where there are enough customers in a small area to make the service profitable. A farm shop, by contrast, targets rural customers who want locally sourced produce.

Segmenting by Demographics

Demographics means “statistical data relating to the population and particular groups within it.” Businesses can segment their market by age, gender, family size, ethnicity, religion, or occupation. For example, a publisher knows that not everyone wants to read the same book — a children’s fiction range targets a completely different demographic to a business management title.

Age: Toddlers (0–3) need soft-tip cutlery and nursery-safe wipes. Pre-teens (9–12) want kids’ smartwatches with GPS. Retirees (65+) look for bigger-button phones and pharmacy subscriptions.

Family setup: Single adults buy meal kits for one and studio-sized furniture. Large families (4+ children) need 12-pack cereals and 7-seater car deals.

Religion & ethnicity: Observant Muslim customers may look for halal meal boxes and Ramadan evening delivery slots. The Black haircare market targets protective-style products and satin pillowcases.

Segmenting by Lifestyle

Customers can be grouped according to the way they lead their lives and the attitudes they share. A young professional may drive a sports car because of the image they want to project, while parents with children need a larger family car to suit their lifestyle. Lifestyle segmentation helps businesses design products that fit the way people actually live.

Holiday companies use lifestyle segmentation extensively. Multi-generational families need villas with pools and kids’ clubs. Pet owners want pet-friendly cottages with nearby walks. Adventure backpackers aged 18–25 look for hostels, group treks, and budget city-to-city passes.

Segmenting by Income

The population can be segmented according to annual salary or type of job. Establishing a group’s disposable income is important so that products can be targeted to the relevant income group. For example, Toyota sells the Aygo at £15,000 for budget-conscious buyers, the RAV4 at £44,000 for middle-income families, and the Supra at £57,000 for high-income enthusiasts.

The UK uses a social class classification system based on occupation. Group A includes upper-class professionals such as lawyers and accountants. Group B covers middle-class professionals like teachers and nurses. Group C1 is lower middle-class skilled non-manual workers such as police officers and clerical staff. Group C2 covers skilled working-class workers like plumbers and electricians. Group D includes unskilled manual workers such as labourers. Group E covers those on state benefits, including pensioners and the unemployed.

A business may decide to target ABC1 consumers with premium products or DE consumers with budget alternatives, depending on the product.

Key Fact

Disposable income is what a person has left after all bills and taxes have been paid. Businesses must identify their target group’s disposable income level to price products correctly — a premium gym membership will not sell to students with very little disposable income.

Market Mapping

Market mapping is the process of finding the variables that differentiate brands in a market and then plotting them on a diagram. The two axes could be price versus quality, functional versus luxury, or modern versus traditional — the choice depends on the industry.

For example, plotting shoe brands on a market map with price on one axis and quality on the other might show Jimmy Choo in the premium/luxury corner, Nike in the mid-price/high-quality area, Primark in the budget/functional area, and a possible gap in the mid-price/luxury space where no brand currently operates.

Identify gaps in the market: If no brand occupies a particular position on the map, that space could represent an opportunity. A start-up can use this to decide what products to launch.

Understand the competition: Plotting competitors helps a business see where the market is crowded and where it might face less direct competition.

Reposition a brand: An established business can use market mapping to see whether it needs to move its brand. The North Face started as professional climbing gear but repositioned itself as a fashion brand through collaborations with Supreme and Gucci, shifting its position on the market map from functional/premium to fashionable/premium.

Key Fact

A market map always has two axes. Exam questions may ask you to draw one, label the axes, or explain what a gap on the map means. Remember: a gap does not guarantee success — there might be no demand in that space.

Benefits & Risks of Segmentation

Segmenting a market allows a business to focus its marketing spend on the customers most likely to buy. It reduces waste because advertising reaches the right people rather than everyone. A segmented approach also helps businesses tailor products to specific needs, which can increase customer satisfaction and loyalty.

However, there are risks. Segmenting too narrowly can exclude potential customers. A personal trainer who targets only high-income clients in a small area might not find enough customers to fill her diary. There is also a cost to researching and understanding each segment — smaller businesses may not have the resources to do this effectively.

What Is the Competitive Environment?

Every business operates within a competitive environment. The more sellers offering a similar product or service, the more intense the competition becomes. For example, the UK fast food market includes McDonald’s, KFC, Burger King, Subway, and many independent outlets — all competing for the same customers.

A competitive market is generally good news for customers. It gives them more choice, keeps prices down, and pushes businesses to invest in research and development (R&D) to keep improving their products. However, for the businesses themselves, competition creates pressure to stand out or risk losing sales.

Key Fact

A competitive environment is the dynamic external system in which a business competes and functions. The more competitors selling similar products, the harder each business must work to attract and keep customers.

Strengths and Weaknesses of Competitors

To succeed in a competitive market, a business needs to understand what its rivals do well and where they fall short. The Edexcel specification identifies five key areas for comparing competitors: price, quality, location, product range, and customer service.

Price: How much the customer is charged for a product or service. Do not confuse price with cost — price is what the customer pays, while cost is what the business spends to make the product. In markets where products are very similar, such as the UK car market, a price war can break out as firms try to undercut each other.

Quality: The standard of materials, design, and reliability of a product. Competing on quality costs more because higher-quality raw materials and processes increase production costs. However, some businesses such as Ryanair and Primark have succeeded by deliberately lowering quality to offer ultra-low prices — this only works if the product is still fit for purpose and price is the main attraction.

Location: Where the business is situated and how easy it is to reach. Convenient locations attract more footfall. For example, Greggs and Costa locate on high streets and near stations for grab-and-go customers, while IKEA and B&Q choose retail parks where there is space for large stores and free parking.

Product range: The variety of products a business offers. A wider range attracts more customers and increases basket size. Amazon’s “everything store” approach means customers have fewer reasons to shop elsewhere, while Zara refreshes its fashion lines weekly to keep customers coming back.

Customer service: How customers are treated before, during, and after a sale. Excellent service builds loyalty, generates positive word-of-mouth, and can justify slightly higher prices. John Lewis is known for friendly staff and easy returns, while First Direct wins awards for its call centre service.

Key Fact

Good customer service creates a chain of benefits: repeat purchases rise, online reviews improve, new customers are attracted, and the business can even charge a small price premium because the service adds value. Example: Apple Store staff provide advice, setup help, and repairs — customers accept premium pricing because of the service experience.

Case Study: Tesco vs Aldi

Comparing two major UK supermarkets shows how different businesses compete on different factors. Tesco competes on product range (food, clothing, pharmacy, online grocery) and location (large Extras plus small Express stores near homes). Aldi competes on price (everyday low prices, fewer promotions) and quality (award-winning own-brand products). Each has found a competitive approach that works for its target customers.

The Impact of Competition on Business Decisions

When competition intensifies, businesses cannot simply carry on as before. They must adapt their decision-making to survive and grow. The specification identifies five key responses.

Make the brand stand out: A strong brand gives a business competitive advantage. If customers recognise and trust the brand, the business can charge higher prices, increasing sales revenue and profit. Those retained profits can then fund further expansion.

Be customer orientated: Being customer orientated means placing customer satisfaction at the heart of every decision. This could mean recruiting and training customer-friendly staff with strong communication and problem-solving skills.

Build customer loyalty: It is much cheaper to sell to an existing customer than to attract a new one. Loyalty programmes such as the Tesco Clubcard or Boots Advantage Card encourage repeat purchases. They also provide valuable data on buying patterns that helps the business target customers more effectively.

Differentiate the product or service: Differentiation means making your product or service distinct from competitors. This can be achieved through design, packaging, targeting a particular market segment, adding new features, or choosing a unique pricing strategy. For example, Burger King differentiates from McDonald’s by flame-grilling its burgers instead of frying them.

Add value to the product or service: Value is added when the customer perceives the extra benefit and is prepared to pay more. This can happen through processes (such as slicing and canning carrots) or through packaging (such as single-portion convenience packs). Free next-day delivery is another way to add value without changing the product itself.

SWOT Analysis in a Competitive Market

A SWOT analysis helps a business make informed decisions by examining its competitive position. Strengths and weaknesses are internal factors the business can control, while opportunities and threats are external factors in the market.

For example, when KFC considered opening a new restaurant in a town 40 miles from the nearest branch, a SWOT analysis revealed: Strengths — famous brand, no nearby KFC competitor; Weaknesses — many existing fast-food rivals; Opportunities — 50,000 residents plus market-day visitors, cafés closing at 5pm leaving evening demand; Threats — 24-hour McDonald’s and multiple takeaways already operating.

Key Fact

Before starting up, an entrepreneur should analyse competitors’ strengths and weaknesses. This helps identify gaps in the market, understand the level of competition, and determine the best strategy for securing market share. A market map can visualise where competitors sit on factors like price and quality.

Direct and Indirect Competition

Direct competition comes from businesses selling the same type of product to the same market — for example, Tesco and Aldi both sell groceries. Indirect competition comes from businesses offering different products that satisfy the same customer need — for example, a cinema and a bowling alley both compete for leisure spending. Understanding both types helps a business see the full picture of its competitive environment.

before.content_html:
What Are Business Aims and Objectives?

Every business needs a clear sense of direction. An aim is a broad, long-term goal that a business wants to achieve. An objective is a specific, shorter-term target that helps a business reach its aim. For example, a business might have the aim of “becoming profitable” and set the objective of “increasing sales by 10% in the next year.”

Key Fact

An aim is a big, long-term goal (e.g. “to grow the business”). An objective is a specific, short- to medium-term target that helps a business reach its aim (e.g. “increase sales by 10% this year”). Objectives give aims a measurable focus.

Businesses set aims and objectives for three important reasons. First, they provide specific targets against which performance can be measured. Second, they help motivate workers by giving them clear goals to work towards. Third, they clarify direction and help managers make better decisions about where to invest time and money.

Financial Aims and Objectives

Financial aims and objectives focus on the money side of a business. The Edexcel specification identifies five key financial aims for businesses starting up: survival, profit, sales, market share, and financial security.

In its first year of trading, many businesses simply aim to survive. This means the owner wants the business to keep trading long enough to become established. To survive, the business needs to reach a sustainable level of sales that covers its costs — in other words, it needs to reach its break-even point. This often means keeping prices low at first. Profit may be small initially, but once the business is established it can raise prices with more confidence.

Profit is total revenue minus total costs (P = TR − TC). A business aiming to maximise profit must either increase the revenue coming in or reduce the costs going out — or ideally both. Profit is essential because it rewards the owner for the risk they have taken and provides funds for reinvestment and growth.

Sales: A new business may set an objective to grow its sales volume. For example, an online shop might keep prices low to attract customers and encourage repeat purchases. Growing sales helps build the customer base that the business needs to survive long-term.

Market share: Market share is the percentage of total sales in a market held by one business. To increase market share, a business must take sales away from competitors. This could be achieved through heavy promotion, discounts, or making products more appealing. In 2019, ASDA attempted to merge with Sainsbury’s to overtake Tesco as the UK’s largest supermarket group, but the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) blocked the deal because it would reduce competition and could lead to higher prices for shoppers.

Financial security: If an entrepreneur has left a regular paid job to start a business, they need the business to generate enough income to cover personal bills such as mortgage payments, loans, and household costs. Financial security means the business provides a reliable, stable income for its owner.

Non-Financial Aims and Objectives

Not every business goal is about money. Non-financial aims focus on personal fulfilment and making a positive difference. The specification identifies five non-financial aims: social objectives, personal satisfaction, challenge, independence, and control.

Key Fact

Financial aims include survival, profit, sales, market share, and financial security. Non-financial aims include social objectives, personal satisfaction, challenge, independence, and control. You must be able to classify each aim correctly in the exam.

Social objectives: Social enterprises are businesses that trade for social or environmental purposes. Their social mission is central to everything they do. For example, Mecoco is a social enterprise that works with disabled adults and young people to create scented home fragrance products, providing meaningful employment opportunities regardless of support needs.

Personal satisfaction: Many entrepreneurs start a business because they want to do something they are passionate about. Working for yourself can provide a deep sense of achievement and fulfilment that a regular job might not offer.

Challenge: Some people are motivated by the challenge of building something from scratch. The idea of a predictable 9-to-5 job does not suit their personality, and they thrive on the unpredictability and problem-solving that comes with running a business.

Independence: Entrepreneurs may want the freedom to make their own decisions rather than working for someone else. Being their own boss means they can shape the business exactly as they want.

Control: Owning a business gives entrepreneurs more control over their working lives. They can choose their own working hours, decide what products or services to sell, and determine how the business is promoted.

Why Aims and Objectives Differ Between Businesses

Private sector businesses (manufacturers, retailers, banks) are owned by private investors and typically aim to maximise profits, increase market share, and expand. Public sector organisations (the BBC, NHS, state schools) are owned by the government and aim to meet customer targets (e.g. reducing patient waiting times) while keeping costs low. Voluntary sector organisations (charities, community groups) aim to increase donations, reduce costs, and provide for those in need. Social enterprises like the Big Issue fall into this category too.

A small sole trader — such as a local plumber — is likely to prioritise survival, personal satisfaction, and financial security. A large PLC like Tesco focuses on increasing market share, maximising profit, and growing sales revenue. The scale and ownership structure of a business directly shapes which aims matter most.

Key Fact

The sector a business operates in (private, public, or voluntary) and its size both influence which aims and objectives it prioritises. A start-up sole trader has very different goals from a multinational PLC.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how a business owner should spend their profit from the first year of trading.
practice_questions.marks:
Upper band (4-6): Developed discussion with at least two ways of spending profit, with analysis of advantages and/or disadvantages. Reaches a justified conclusion.
• Reinvest in the business (e.g. redecorate premises, buy new equipment) to attract more customers and grow.
• Save the profit as a financial buffer in case of unexpected costs or a difficult trading period.
• Take the profit out as personal income — the owner may need to reward themselves for the risk taken.
• Spend on marketing/loyalty schemes to protect against future competition.
Lower band (1-3): Basic identification or limited explanation of one or two uses of profit.
Conclusion might argue: In the first year, reinvesting is usually the better choice because the business needs to establish itself and build a customer base, which will generate higher profits in future years.

practice_questions.text: Fixed costs for a business are £26,000 per year. Variable costs include wages at £10 per unit, raw materials at £12 per unit and delivery at £3 per unit. The business expects to sell 750 units at £26 each. Justify whether the business should go ahead with production. You are advised to show your workings.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-9): Detailed justification with accurate calculations, clear analysis of the financial position, and a reasoned conclusion.
Calculations:
• Variable cost per unit = £10 + £12 + £3 = £25
• Total variable costs = 750 × £25 = £18,750
• Total costs = £26,000 + £18,750 = £44,750
• Revenue = 750 × £26 = £19,500
• Loss = £19,500 – £44,750 = –£25,250
Analysis: The business would make a loss of £25,250. The selling price (£26) barely covers the variable cost per unit (£25), leaving only £1 per unit towards fixed costs. To break even, the business would need to sell far more units or increase its selling price.
However, the business might still go ahead if it expects sales to grow significantly in future years, or if it can reduce costs. Some businesses accept initial losses as part of building a customer base.
Mid band (4-6): Correct calculations with some analysis but limited justification.
Lower band (1-3): Attempts calculations with limited or no analysis.

before.content_html:
What Is Break-Even?

When a business starts up, the owner invests money in equipment, fixtures, and stock. At first, there is little or no revenue coming in, but costs are already building up. The business needs to know the point at which it stops making a loss and starts covering all of its costs. This point is called break-even.

At break-even, total revenue is exactly equal to total costs. The business is not making a profit, but it is not making a loss either. Every unit sold beyond the break-even point generates profit, while selling fewer units than the break-even point means the business is making a loss.

Key Fact

Break-even is the point where total costs = total revenue. The business makes neither a profit nor a loss. Every unit sold above break-even generates profit.

Why Is Break-Even Analysis Useful?

Break-even analysis is a powerful planning tool for businesses. It helps owners and managers make better decisions about pricing, costs, and output levels. There are three main reasons a business uses break-even analysis:

  • Starting up: A new business can work out how many units it needs to sell before it stops making a loss. This information is essential for planning.
  • “What if?” scenarios: Break-even analysis can be used to explore what happens if prices rise, costs increase, or demand changes. This helps the business prepare for different situations.
  • Attracting investors: Banks and investors want to see break-even figures in a business plan. It shows the business has calculated when it will become profitable.

The Break-Even Formula

To calculate the break-even level of output, you need three pieces of information: fixed costs, selling price per unit, and variable cost per unit. The formula is:

Key Fact

Break-even level of output = Fixed costs ÷ (Selling price − Variable cost per unit)

The bottom part of the formula (selling price minus variable cost) is called the contribution per unit. This is the amount each unit sold contributes towards covering fixed costs.

Contribution per unit tells you how much money from each sale goes towards covering fixed costs. Once enough units have been sold to cover all fixed costs, the business has reached break-even.

A business has fixed costs of £25,000. Each unit sells for £450. The variable cost per unit is £280.

Step 1: Calculate the contribution per unit: £450 − £280 = £170

Step 2: Apply the formula: £25,000 ÷ £170 = 147.06

Step 3: Round up to the nearest whole unit: 148 units

The business must produce and sell 148 units to break even. Always round up — you cannot sell part of a product, and rounding down would leave the business short of covering its costs.

Note that break-even is always expressed in units, not in pounds. It tells you how many products you need to sell, not how much money you need to make.

Reading a Break-Even Diagram

A break-even diagram (also called a break-even chart) is a graph that shows the relationship between costs, revenue, and output. It plots three lines:

  • Fixed costs (FC): A horizontal line because fixed costs do not change with output.
  • Total costs (TC): Starts at the fixed costs level (because even at zero output, fixed costs must be paid) and rises as output increases, since variable costs are added on top.
  • Total revenue (TR): Starts at the origin (zero output means zero revenue) and rises as more units are sold.

The break-even point is where the total revenue line crosses the total costs line. To the left of this point, total costs are higher than total revenue, so the business is making a loss. To the right of this point, total revenue exceeds total costs, so the business is making a profit.

Key Fact

On a break-even diagram: the area to the left of the break-even point represents a loss, and the area to the right represents a profit. The break-even point is where the TR and TC lines cross.

Margin of Safety

The margin of safety tells a business how many sales it can afford to lose before it starts making a loss. A large margin of safety means the business is in a comfortable position. A small margin of safety means even a slight drop in sales could push the business into a loss.

Key Fact

Margin of safety = Actual sales − Break-even sales

The answer is expressed in units. A higher margin of safety means less risk for the business.

A shop has actual sales of 425 units per month. Its break-even point is 250 units.

Margin of safety = 425 − 250 = 175 units

This means the shop could lose up to 175 sales per month before it would start making a loss. This is a healthy margin of safety.

The Impact of Changes in Costs and Revenue

Break-even is not a fixed number — it changes whenever costs or revenue change. Understanding how different factors shift the break-even point is a key exam skill.

If fixed costs rise: The FC line shifts upward on the diagram, which pushes the TC line up too. The break-even point moves to the right, meaning the business must sell more units to cover costs. The margin of safety decreases.

If variable costs fall: The TC line pivots downward (it becomes less steep). The break-even point moves to the left, meaning fewer units need to be sold. The margin of safety increases.

If selling price increases: The TR line becomes steeper, crossing the TC line sooner. The break-even point moves to the left, and the margin of safety increases. However, a higher price may reduce demand.

If selling price decreases: The TR line becomes less steep, crossing the TC line later. The break-even point moves to the right, and the margin of safety shrinks.

In the exam, you may be asked to explain how a business could lower its break-even point. The two main strategies are: reduce total costs (for example, by finding a cheaper supplier to lower variable costs) or increase the selling price (so each unit contributes more towards fixed costs). Both options have trade-offs that need to be evaluated.

Meringue is a bakery in a busy town centre with a strong reputation for high-quality bread and pastries. The owners want to reduce their break-even point. They have two options:

Option 1 — Increase prices by 10%: Because Meringue has strong customer loyalty and positive reviews, many customers are likely to keep buying even at slightly higher prices. On the break-even chart, the TR line would rise more steeply, crossing TC sooner and reducing the break-even level of output. However, some price-sensitive customers may switch to cheaper competitors nearby.

Option 2 — Use cheaper ingredients: This would lower variable costs and shift the TC line down, reducing break-even. However, cheaper ingredients could lower quality, damaging the bakery’s reputation and leading to fewer sales — which could actually make it harder to reach break-even in the long term.
before.exam_tip_html: For break-even questions, always show your workings clearly — even if you get the wrong final answer, you can still pick up method marks. Remember to express your answer in units, not pounds, and always round up to the nearest whole unit. In “Explain” questions about reducing break-even, use a clear chain of reasoning: identify the change (e.g. lower variable costs), explain the mechanism (contribution per unit increases), and state the impact (break-even point falls, fewer units needed to cover costs).
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Break-even is the level of output where total costs equal total revenue — the formula is fixed costs ÷ (selling price − variable cost per unit), and the answer is always in units.
  • The margin of safety shows how many sales a business can lose before making a loss, calculated as actual sales minus break-even sales.
  • Changes in fixed costs, variable costs, or selling price all shift the break-even point and margin of safety — understanding these shifts is essential for exam diagram interpretation questions.

practice_questions.text: Discuss whether break-even analysis is useful for a business that is starting up.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks using a points-based approach.

Arguments for:
• Helps the business calculate how many units it needs to sell to cover costs, so the owner can plan production levels and sales targets.
• Can be included in a business plan to show banks or investors that the business has a clear financial plan, making it more likely to secure a loan.
• Acts as a 'what if?' tool, allowing the business to see the impact of changing prices or costs before they happen.

Arguments against:
• Based on estimates — a start-up may not know its exact costs or selling price yet, so the break-even figure could be inaccurate.
• Assumes all output is sold, which is unlikely for a new business with no established customer base.
• Does not account for changes over time — costs and prices are likely to change as the business grows.

For full marks, students must consider both sides and reach a supported conclusion.

practice_questions.text:
Sandwell Sheds Ltd has fixed costs of £1,000 per month. It sells sheds at an average price of £200. Average variable costs per shed are £160.

Justify which of the following options Sandwell Sheds should choose to reduce its break-even level of output:

Option 1: Negotiate a £200 reduction in monthly rent (fixed costs)
Option 2: Find a cheaper timber supplier, reducing variable costs by £20 per shed
practice_questions.marks:
Use the P-A-BLT + AIM framework.
For Option 1 (reduce fixed costs by £200):
• Current break-even: £1,000 ÷ (£200 – £160) = 25 sheds
• New break-even: £800 ÷ £40 = 20 sheds
• Reduces break-even by 5 sheds. Guaranteed saving as rent is a fixed cost.
For Option 2 (reduce variable costs by £20):
• New break-even: £1,000 ÷ (£200 – £140) = £1,000 ÷ £60 = 16.67 = 17 sheds
• Reduces break-even by 8 sheds. Greater impact but depends on quality.
Conclusion: Option 2 has a bigger impact on break-even (17 vs 20 sheds). However, it depends on whether cheaper timber affects the quality of the sheds. If quality drops, customers may stop buying. The most important factor is maintaining product quality — if the cheaper supplier can match current standards, Option 2 is better because it reduces break-even more and also increases the contribution per unit on every shed sold.
Top band (7-9): Justified recommendation with calculations, application to context, and consideration of both options.
Mid band (4-6): Some analysis of options with limited application.
Lower band (1-3): Basic points with limited development.

before.content_html:
What Is Interest?

When a business does not have enough money to fund its plans, it borrows money — usually from a bank. The business must pay back the original amount it borrowed plus an extra charge called interest. Interest is written as a percentage (%) of the amount borrowed, and it is how banks and lenders make their money.

Key Fact

Interest can be applied to many types of borrowing: bank loans, mortgages, credit cards, store cards, car leasing, and buy-now-pay-later schemes. Any time money is borrowed, the lender charges interest as the cost of lending.

Calculating Interest on a Loan

In the Edexcel exam, you need to be able to calculate the interest rate on a loan. The formula is:

Key Fact

Interest (%) = (Total Repayment − Borrowed Amount) ÷ Borrowed Amount × 100

Here is a worked example. A business borrows £10,000 over 10 years and pays £179.94 per month. First, calculate the total repayment: £179.94 × 120 months = £21,592.80. Then apply the formula: (£21,592.80 − £10,000) ÷ £10,000 × 100 = 115.93%. This means the business pays back more than double what it originally borrowed.

Example 1: John borrows £10,000 and pays £300 per month for 3 years. Total repayment = £300 × 36 = £10,800. Interest = (£10,800 − £10,000) ÷ £10,000 × 100 = 8%.

Example 2: Kim borrows £25,000 and pays £500 per month for 6 years. Total repayment = £500 × 72 = £36,000. Interest = (£36,000 − £25,000) ÷ £25,000 × 100 = 44%.

Notice that longer repayment periods lead to higher total interest, even if the monthly payment seems affordable.

The Impact of Rising Interest Rates

Most businesses need to borrow money at some point — to start up, buy equipment, or fund expansion. When interest rates rise, the cost of repaying loans increases. Loan repayments are a fixed cost, so higher interest rates push up a business’s total costs and reduce its profit. Businesses can try to plan for this, but unexpected rate rises can cause serious problems.

Why Is Cash Important to a Business?

Cash is the money a business has available to pay its bills right now. The exam board highlights four reasons cash is essential:

Key Fact

Cash is needed to: (1) pay suppliers — without payment, suppliers stop delivering raw materials; (2) pay overheads — rent, utilities, and insurance must be paid or services get cut off; (3) pay employees — unpaid staff will leave, increasing labour turnover; (4) prevent insolvency — a business that cannot pay its debts when they are due is insolvent and may be forced to close.

Cash vs Profit

Cash and profit are not the same thing. Profit is what remains after total costs are deducted from total revenue (Profit = TR − TC). Cash is the money actually available in the bank right now. A business can be profitable on paper but still run out of cash. This happens because customers do not always pay immediately — they may receive an invoice and pay 30, 60, or even 90 days later. During that wait, the business still has bills to pay.

Cash Flow Forecasts

A cash flow forecast is a table that predicts the movement of cash into and out of a business over a future period, usually a year. It is included in a business plan and helps the business spot months where it might face a shortfall.

A cash flow forecast has five key components:

1. Cash inflows — money coming in, mainly from sales revenue. Other inflows include bank loans, owner’s capital, and government grants.

2. Cash outflows — money leaving the business, such as stock purchases, wages, rent, utilities, advertising, and interest payments on loans.

3. Net cash flow — the difference between inflows and outflows. Net Cash Flow = Cash Inflows − Cash Outflows. A negative figure means more cash went out than came in.

4. Opening balance — the cash the business has at the start of the period, carried forward from the previous month’s closing balance.

5. Closing balance — the cash at the end of the period. Closing Balance = Opening Balance + Net Cash Flow. If this is negative, the business needs additional finance such as an overdraft.

Key Fact

Key formulas: Net Cash Flow = Cash Inflows − Cash Outflows. Closing Balance = Opening Balance + Net Cash Flow. In the exam, when calculating net cash flow, ignore opening and closing balances.

Interpreting a Cash Flow Forecast

Interpreting a cash flow forecast means reading the numbers and explaining what they tell you about the business. Look for months with negative net cash flow or a negative closing balance — these are danger points where the business may need to borrow money. A seasonal business like a fancy dress shop will see high inflows around Halloween and New Year, but quiet months in between where outflows exceed inflows.

If a business has a cash shortfall, it can take action on both sides of the forecast:

Increase inflows: arrange an overdraft for short-term cover, offer discounts and promotions to boost sales, or reduce the credit period given to customers so they pay faster.

Reduce outflows: cut unnecessary costs, reduce waste, switch to cheaper suppliers, or negotiate trade credit with suppliers so the business has longer to pay its own bills.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the importance of cash flow forecasting for a seasonal business such as a fancy dress shop.
practice_questions.marks:
Content: up to 3 marks. Application: up to 3 marks.
Indicative content:
• A cash flow forecast shows expected inflows and outflows month by month (1). For a fancy dress shop, sales peak at Halloween and New Year but are much lower in other months (1). The forecast identifies quiet months where outflows may exceed inflows, creating a negative net cash flow (1).
• The business can plan ahead — for example, saving surplus cash from busy months, arranging an overdraft, or reducing stock orders in quiet months (1). Without a forecast the business might not realise it will run short of cash until it is too late to act (1). This reduces the risk of insolvency and helps the business survive seasonal fluctuations (1).

practice_questions.text: A start-up café borrows £15,000 from the bank at an interest rate that results in total repayments of £19,500 over five years. The café's cash flow forecast shows a negative closing balance in three of the first six months. Justify whether the café should go ahead with the loan. You should consider both sides of your argument before reaching a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 9 marks using a levels-based approach:
Top band (7-9): Thorough analysis of both sides with a justified conclusion linked to the context. Shows understanding of both interest costs and cash flow implications.
Mid band (4-6): Some analysis of advantages and disadvantages. Limited application to context.
Lower band (1-3): Limited points with little development.
Indicative content:
For: The café needs equipment/stock to trade — without the loan it cannot open (1). The interest rate is (£19,500 − £15,000) ÷ £15,000 × 100 = 30% over 5 years, which is moderate for a start-up (1). Once established, sales revenue should improve cash inflows (1).
Against: Three negative closing balances in six months means the café may struggle to pay suppliers and staff (1). Loan repayments are a fixed cost that must be paid even in quiet months, worsening cash flow (1). Rising interest rates in future could increase costs further (1).
Conclusion should weigh both sides, e.g. the loan is justified if the café can arrange an overdraft for the difficult months and has a realistic plan for growing revenue.
