before.content_html:
Limited and Unlimited Liability

Before choosing a type of business ownership, every entrepreneur needs to understand liability. Liability means who is responsible for paying debts if a business owes money. There are two types: limited and unlimited.

Key Fact

Unlimited liability means the business and the owner are one legal entity. If the business cannot pay its debts, the owner must pay from their own personal money, savings, and possessions — including their house and car. Limited liability means the owner can only lose the money they invested in the business. Their personal belongings are protected.

For example, imagine a business owes £10,000 but only has £2,000 in the bank. With unlimited liability, the owner could be chased for the remaining £8,000 from their personal funds. With limited liability, the owner usually only loses what they put into the business.

Businesses are classified as either unincorporated (sole traders and partnerships — unlimited liability) or incorporated (private limited companies — limited liability). An incorporated business is a separate legal entity from its owners.

Sole Traders

A sole trader (also called a sole proprietor) is a person who starts, owns, and runs a business on their own. They are the only owner, although they can hire staff to work for them. These staff have no ownership or control over the business. A sole trader does not issue shares.

Common examples of sole trader businesses include plumbers, electricians, hairdressers, cleaners, and website designers. Many small, local businesses operate as sole traders.

Advantages: The owner can make decisions quickly without needing agreement from others. All profits are kept by the owner and do not need to be shared. The owner can offer personal attention to customers. There is no requirement to make company information public. The owner is their own boss.

Disadvantages: It is difficult to raise money — banks may see a sole trader as a higher risk. There are no economies of scale, for example buying in bulk. There is no one to take over during ill health or holidays. The owner has no one to share ideas or problems with. They rely on only one set of skills. Most importantly, sole traders have unlimited liability.

Partnerships

A partnership is a business with two or more owners who are joint owners. Partners share decision-making, although they may also employ a manager to help run the business. Like sole traders, partnerships have unlimited liability.

Common partnership businesses include dentists, accountants, solicitors, and vets — professions where partners need to trust each other and bring specialist skills. Profits are distributed based on the percentage each partner has invested. For example, if one partner invested 30% of the total capital, they receive 30% of the profits.

Advantages: Easier to raise capital than a sole trader because more partners can invest. Partners share problems and decisions, reducing the burden on any one person. Partners bring a range of skills — for example, a dental practice might have a dentist, a hygienist, and an orthodontist. Banks may be more willing to lend to a partnership because there are more people to repay the debt. No need to make financial information public.

Disadvantages: Partnerships have unlimited liability, meaning personal assets are at risk. Trust and reliability between partners can be an issue. Disagreements between partners can make business decisions difficult. A deed of partnership must be produced, which is expensive and adds to start-up costs. If one partner wants to leave, it can force changes or even end the partnership.

Private Limited Companies (Ltd)

A private limited company (Ltd) is a business that can raise finance by selling shares, but only privately to friends and family — not to the general public. The business has limited liability, which means owners’ personal assets are protected if the business gets into debt.

Private limited companies are often family businesses that started as sole traders and grew. Once they become a Ltd, they can sell shares to raise further capital for expansion. Examples include many small to medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) such as builders, roofers, electricians, and garden services.

Key Fact

Private limited companies benefit from limited liability — investors can only lose the amount they invested, not their personal possessions. Banks are also more willing to lend to a Ltd than to a sole trader or partnership. However, the business must prepare annual accounts and make them available to the public, which is expensive and lets competitors see financial information.

Advantages: Protection of limited liability for investors. Easier to raise capital by issuing more shares to friends and family. Banks are more willing to lend money. Easier to grow and expand because there is more capital available.

Disadvantages: The business must issue more information about itself, which can be expensive to produce. Annual accounts must be prepared, printed, and sent to all shareholders. These accounts must also be made available for the general public and competitors to see. Selling shares means control can be diluted — majority shareholders may have a say in major decisions.

Franchises

A franchise is when an established business (the franchisor) sells the right to another person (the franchisee) to trade using its brand name, logo, products, and business systems. The franchisee pays an initial fee plus ongoing royalty payments based on their sales revenue.

For example, a Subway franchise in the UK costs around £13,000 as an initial franchise fee, with a total investment starting at approximately £150,000. On top of this, Subway charges around 8% royalty fees plus 4.5% advertising fees — totalling 12.5% of gross sales.

Key Fact

A franchise is often described as a “business in a box” because the franchisee gets an established brand, training, equipment, marketing support, and proven systems. However, they must follow the franchisor’s rules on products, branding, layout, and suppliers.

Advantages for the franchisee: The business benefits from national or worldwide advertising paid for by the franchisor. Market research is done at head office level. There is less competition because territories are divided up between franchisees. The brand name and reputation are already well known, making it easier to attract customers. Training and support from the franchisor reduces risk compared to starting from scratch.

Disadvantages for the franchisee: The owner has less control because they must follow the franchisor’s rules on promotions, products, and operations. Ongoing royalty fees reduce profit. The initial franchise fee and set-up costs can be very high. The franchisee cannot easily differentiate their business from others in the franchise.

Choosing the Right Type of Ownership

The best type of business ownership depends on several factors: how much risk the entrepreneur is willing to take, how much capital they need, whether they want full control or are willing to share decision-making, and how much they want to protect their personal assets. A sole trader keeps all profits but faces unlimited liability. A partnership allows shared skills and finance but can lead to disagreements. A private limited company offers limited liability but requires more paperwork and public disclosure. A franchise provides an established brand but limits independence and requires ongoing fees.

lessons.title: Business Location and the Marketing Mix

before.content_html:
Why Does Business Location Matter?

Where a business chooses to locate is one of the most important decisions an entrepreneur makes. The right location can reduce costs, attract customers, and give the business a competitive edge. The wrong location can mean high costs, low footfall, and ultimately business failure. Several key factors influence this decision.

Key Fact

The four main factors influencing business location are: proximity to market (being near customers), proximity to labour (access to skilled or affordable workers), proximity to materials (being near raw materials to cut transport costs), and proximity to competitors (clustering near rivals to attract shared footfall).

Proximity to Market

Being close to customers is essential for many businesses. Convenience goods like bread and milk need to be sold where people already shop, such as high streets or residential areas. Bulky or perishable goods manufacturers must locate near customers because transporting these products long distances is expensive or impractical.

Consumer goods manufacturers such as Unilever reduce transport costs by locating factories close to their customers around the world. Retail businesses benefit from high footfall — the more people passing by, the more potential sales. Services like nearby nurseries and shops also attract employees, making the location more appealing to workers.

Proximity to Labour

Businesses need an adequate supply of workers with the right skills. Some businesses deliberately locate in areas of high unemployment to access a large pool of applicants. This can keep wage costs lower and make recruitment faster. A call centre, for example, might choose a city location to access a large labour pool.

However, relocating to an area with fewer skilled workers can lead to higher training costs and lower productivity. Businesses must balance wage savings against the quality and availability of labour in the area.

Proximity to Materials

For manufacturers, being close to raw materials reduces transport costs and the risk of supply delays. Bulk-reducing products — where the finished product is smaller than the raw materials — benefit most from locating near their material source.

Denby Pottery is based in Denby, Derbyshire, because a large seam of high-quality clay was discovered there. The area was also historically rich in coal, which provided fuel for firing kilns. Being close to raw materials cut transport costs and ensured a reliable supply. Good transport links into nearby towns and cities helped Denby distribute its finished products to customers.

Proximity to Competitors

Some businesses deliberately locate near their competitors. This is known as the cluster concept. For example, the Birmingham Jewellery Quarter draws customers looking for jewellery — if they cannot find what they want in one shop, they try another nearby. However, clustering can also lead to price wars and reduced profit margins as businesses compete for the same customers.

The Nature of Business Activity and Location

The type of business also affects the best location. Retail businesses need high footfall areas like shopping centres, though rents there are higher. Service businesses may not need a physical premises — a gardener or web designer can work from home but must travel to clients. Manufacturing businesses need good transport links (roads, ports, airports) and access to skilled labour. Some manufacturers locate where government grants are available, such as Toyota’s factory in Derby.

Many entrepreneurs start small to reduce risk — working from home, starting from a market stall, or launching online. Levi Roots started his sauce business from his kitchen, selling at the Notting Hill Carnival before growing into a national brand.

The Impact of the Internet on Location

The rise of e-commerce has transformed location decisions. Entrepreneurs can now run businesses from home using platforms like eBay, Etsy, and Amazon. E-commerce offers lower operating costs (no rent on premises), the ability to reach a wider audience, and 24/7 trading. However, online-only businesses are “hidden” — customers may not discover them without effective promotion.

Key Fact

Fixed premises offer face-to-face customer service, the chance to see and try products, and passing trade — but come with high fixed costs like rent and business rates. E-commerce offers lower costs, wider reach, and 24/7 sales — but customers cannot try products and the website could go down, interrupting sales.

The Marketing Mix: The 4Ps

The marketing mix is made up of four elements known as the 4Ps: Product, Price, Place, and Promotion. To get customers to buy, a business needs the right product, at the right price, in the right place, with the right promotion. All four Ps must work together and be consistent with the target market.

Product — the goods or services a business offers. The product must satisfy customer needs. In the marketing mix, “product” also includes services. A small cycle shop’s product mix might include bikes, helmets, water bottles, and clothing.

Price — what the customer pays. The business must be competitive enough to attract customers but charge enough to make a profit. Several pricing strategies exist, from low-cost pricing to premium pricing.

Place — how the product reaches the customer. Options include selling online, opening a shop, selling through other retailers, or selling to wholesalers. Multi-channel distribution means using more than one of these methods.

Promotion — how the business attracts and persuades customers to buy. Methods include price promotions (e.g. £20 off), adding value through bundle deals, and sales promotions with limited-time offers.

How the 4Ps Work Together

The 4Ps must be consistent — they should all match the same target customer and brand position. If one P does not fit, the whole plan falls apart and sales drop. A good marketing mix answers one question: does this product, at this price, in this place, promoted in this way, make sense for the same target customer?

Product: basic wireless earbuds with trendy colours and decent battery life. Price: around £25 (affordable for teens). Place: Amazon, Argos, and supermarkets (easy to access). Promotion: TikTok ads, influencer discount codes, and student deals. This works because everything matches the teen market — the product is affordable, easy to buy, and promoted where teenagers spend their time.

Balancing the Marketing Mix in a Competitive Environment

When there are many competitors, a business can follow one of two strategies. It can be a low-price provider, offering mass market products at low prices (like Home Bargains), with mass media promotion and placement in supermarkets. Alternatively, it can pursue product differentiation, offering unique, higher-priced products for a niche market (like Lush cosmetics), promoted through specialist channels and sold in exclusive locations.

Key Fact

A balanced marketing mix increases sales because all 4Ps fit the same target market. It also improves brand image and loyalty because the promotion, product, and price appear consistent and trustworthy, leading to more repeat customers and positive word of mouth.

Changing Consumer Needs and the Marketing Mix

Consumer needs change over time, and successful businesses adapt their marketing mix to keep up. In the food-to-go market, growing concern about sugar and health has led businesses to offer smaller portions and low-sugar options (product), healthier meal deals (price), healthier options at tills (place), and “low sugar” influencer tie-ins (promotion).

In fashion, sustainability concerns have pushed brands to use recycled materials (product), justify higher prices through durability (price), add online resale sections (place), and run transparency campaigns (promotion). Businesses that fail to adapt risk losing customers to competitors who do.

Technology and the Marketing Mix

Digital communication has changed every element of the marketing mix. Online polls and reviews help businesses improve their product faster. Price comparison websites force businesses to justify their price or offer extra value. Online stores mean businesses can sell anywhere, anytime (place). Social media and targeted advertising allow businesses to reach the right audience quickly and measure results (promotion).

M-commerce (mobile commerce) has grown rapidly, with many consumers now shopping and paying through their phones. Platforms like ASOS Marketplace allow independent sellers to reach niche audiences through an established online platform.

• However, maintaining a balanced mix requires constant adaptation — if consumer needs change, the business must adjust all 4Ps to stay competitive, which takes time and money.

practice_questions.text:
Justify which location factor is most important for a new café business. You should consider:
• proximity to market
• proximity to labour
• proximity to competitors.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-9): Chains of reasoning are complete, analysis is relevant, and conclusion is justified with evidence.
Mid band (4-6): Sound analysis with some justification and context.
Lower band (1-3): Basic analysis with limited context.
Indicative content:
• Proximity to market: A café relies on passing trade and footfall. Being on a busy high street or near offices means more potential customers. Perishable food cannot be transported far, so the café must be near its customers.
• Proximity to labour: A café needs staff who can work flexible hours. Locating near a large population with good transport links makes recruitment easier and keeps wage costs manageable.
• Proximity to competitors: Locating near other food outlets can attract shared footfall (cluster concept), but may lead to price wars and reduced margins.
• Justified conclusion: Proximity to market is most important because without footfall and passing trade, the café will not generate enough sales to survive, regardless of how good its labour supply or competitive position is.

before.content_html:
What Is a Business Plan?

A business plan is a written document that explains a business idea and how it will work in practice. It brings together everything an entrepreneur needs to think about before launching — from the product or service they will sell, to how they will make money, to what could go wrong.

For the Edexcel exam, you will not be asked to write a business plan yourself. However, you must understand the role, importance, and purpose of a business plan, and be able to explain how it helps a business succeed.

Key Fact

A business plan identifies: the business idea, aims and objectives, target market (from market research), forecast revenue/costs/profit, a cash-flow forecast, sources of finance, location, and the marketing mix. These are the eight roles the exam board expects you to know.

The Role and Importance of a Business Plan

A business plan serves several key purposes. First, it forces the entrepreneur to focus on their business idea — what gap in the market they are filling, what product or service they will offer, and who their target customers are. Writing this down makes the idea concrete rather than vague.

Second, it sets out aims and objectives. A well-written plan includes SMART objectives (Specific, Measurable, Agreed, Realistic, Time-limited) so the business has clear goals to work towards. For example, “sell 150 units per week by the end of Month 2” is far more useful than “get loads of customers.”

1. Identify the business idea — What product or service will be sold? What gap in the market does it fill?

2. Business aims and objectives — What are the SMART targets? What does the business want to achieve?

3. Target market — Who are the customers? What does market research show about demand?

4. Forecast revenue, costs and profit — How much money will the business make, spend, and keep?

5. Cash-flow forecast — When will cash come in and go out each month? Are there any shortfall months?

6. Sources of finance — Where will the start-up capital come from? Banks, investors, family, crowdfunding?

7. Location — Where will the business operate? Is it near customers, suppliers, and transport links?

8. Marketing mix — How will the product be priced, promoted, distributed, and what features will it have?

The Purpose of Planning: Reducing Risk and Obtaining Finance

A carefully written business plan reduces the chance of business failure. If the owner has to write down future plans and finances, they are more likely to spot potential problems early. For example, a cash-flow forecast might reveal that the business will run out of cash in Month 3 — allowing the owner to arrange an overdraft or cut costs before it becomes a crisis.

A business plan also helps to obtain finance. Banks, venture capitalists, and angel investors will not lend money unless they can see detailed evidence that the business will grow and generate profit. The better the financial information in the plan, the more confident lenders will be. A plan also helps identify the resources a business needs: human resources (staff), equipment, raw materials, technology, and vehicles.

Stakeholders and Their Interests

A stakeholder is anyone who has an interest in a business. Different stakeholders have different — and sometimes conflicting — interests. For the exam, you need to know six key stakeholder groups and what each one wants from the business.

Key Fact

The six key stakeholders are: customers (want quality products at fair prices), employees (want fair pay, job security, and good working conditions), shareholders (want profit and a return on investment), local community (want jobs, minimal pollution, and community support), government (wants tax revenue, legal compliance, and employment), and suppliers (want regular orders and prompt payment).

Stakeholder interests can conflict. For example, shareholders may want to maximise profits by cutting wages, but employees want higher pay. A business that prioritises ethics tries to meet the wider needs of all its stakeholders, not just the owners.

The Impact of Technology

Technology is a major external influence on business. It creates opportunities for new business ideas — for example, online platforms like Amazon and apps like Uber only exist because of advances in digital technology. It can also make existing products obsolete; film cameras, video rental shops, and traditional chimney sweeps have all declined because of technological change.

Technology also changes the way businesses operate. It improves efficiency through software for payroll, stock control, and document management. It enables remote working, allowing employees to collaborate from anywhere in the world. In production, technology can lower costs, improve quality, increase productivity, and add flexibility — though it often requires significant upfront investment and staff retraining.

Consumer law protects buyers. Key rules include: goods must match any description given, goods must be of satisfactory quality, and adverts must not be misleading. Following consumer law builds customer trust — if a faulty product is replaced or refunded, customers leave positive reviews and return. However, compliance can raise costs for small businesses through staff training and processing returns.

Employment law protects workers. All employees must be paid at least the National Minimum Wage for their age. It is illegal to pay two workers differently for the same job without a good reason (discrimination). Employers hold core responsibility for health and safety in the workplace, though employees must also cooperate. Phrases like “recent graduate” in job adverts risk age discrimination unless the requirement is objectively justified.

Legislation increases costs in the short term (training, compliance, admin), but it also protects the business’s reputation, builds customer loyalty, and helps attract quality job candidates.

The Economy and External Influences

The economy has a powerful effect on business performance. Four key economic factors you need to know are:

Interest rates are the cost of borrowing money. When interest rates rise, businesses pay more to repay loans, increasing their fixed costs and squeezing profits. Higher rates also discourage consumers from borrowing, reducing demand for expensive items like cars and houses.

Exchange rates affect businesses that import or export. If the pound weakens, UK exports become cheaper for foreign buyers (boosting sales abroad), but imported materials cost more. If the pound strengthens, the opposite happens — exports become more expensive and imports become cheaper.

Taxation affects business costs and consumer spending. Higher taxes on businesses reduce profits. Higher income tax or VAT reduces consumers’ disposable income, meaning they spend less. Lower taxes can stimulate spending and growth.

Unemployment affects both demand and labour supply. High unemployment means consumers have less money to spend, reducing demand. However, it can make it easier for businesses to recruit staff because more people are looking for work, and wage demands may be lower.

Key Fact

External influences are factors outside the business’s control that affect its performance. The main ones for Edexcel are: stakeholders, technology, legislation (consumer and employment law), and the economy (interest rates, exchange rates, taxation, unemployment). A business cannot control these but must plan for and respond to them.

Key Takeaways

  • A business plan reduces risk and helps obtain finance by setting out the idea, target market, financial forecasts, location, and marketing mix in a formal document.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'business plan'.
practice_questions.marks: A business plan is a written document that sets out the business idea, aims, financial forecasts, and how the business will operate (1).

practice_questions.text: Outline one way a business plan could help an entrepreneur opening a new restaurant.
practice_questions.marks:
One way is to help secure a bank loan (1). If the entrepreneur provides detailed financial information, the bank can see when the restaurant will be profitable and repay the loan (1).

OR

A business plan helps identify potential risks (1). For example, a cash-flow forecast might show months where the restaurant will have a shortfall, so the owner can arrange finance in advance (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why changes in technology can create new business ideas.
practice_questions.marks:
Point: Changes in technology create new possibilities (1).
Because: New tools such as apps and AI allow businesses to make products or deliver services in new ways (1).
Therefore: New ideas are generated to meet emerging customer needs, such as Uber using GPS technology to offer a cheaper taxi-booking service (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain one impact of rising interest rates on a small business that has a bank loan.
practice_questions.marks:
Point: Rising interest rates increase the cost of borrowing (1).
Because: The business must pay more each month in loan repayments, which are a fixed cost (1).
Therefore: Total costs of production rise, which may reduce profit or force the business to raise prices (1).

practice_questions.text: Discuss whether following consumer law mainly benefits a small independent phone retailer.
practice_questions.marks:
Point A (benefit):
Point: Following consumer law builds customer trust for the phone shop (1).
Because: If a handset is faulty or not as described, the shop offers a repair, replacement, or refund (1).
Therefore: Fewer disputes lead to better reviews and repeat purchases, so sales grow (1).

Point B (drawback):
Point: Complying fully can raise costs for a small retailer (1).
Because: Staff time on checks, training, and processing returns adds admin costs (1).
Therefore: Margins are squeezed unless prices rise, which could put the shop at a disadvantage against larger competitors (1).

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the importance of producing a detailed business plan for a new business start-up.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-9): Detailed analysis with both sides and a justified conclusion.
Arguments for importance:
• Reduces risk of failure by forcing the owner to think through finances, market, and operations before launching.
• Helps obtain finance — banks and investors need to see forecasts of revenue, costs, and profit before lending.
• Identifies resources needed (staff, equipment, materials, technology) so the business is prepared.
• Sets SMART objectives that keep the business focused.
Arguments against / limitations:
• A business plan is based on forecasts which may be inaccurate — actual sales could be very different.
• The business environment is dynamic — external factors like the economy, technology, or legislation can change quickly, making the plan outdated.
• Some successful entrepreneurs have started without a formal plan.
Conclusion: Overall, a business plan is very important for most start-ups because it forces the entrepreneur to research their market, plan their finances, and identify risks before they invest money. Without one, the business is more likely to fail and less likely to secure external funding.
